title: HumAID: Human-Annotated Disaster Incidents Data from Twitter with Deep Learning Benchmarks
venue: Proceedings of the International AAAI Conference on Web and Social Media (ICWSM 2021)
problem_statement: Social media streams generated during disaster events provide time-critical situational information for emergency response, but raw microblog posts contain high volumes of noise, redundancy, and irrelevant content. Existing crisis informatics datasets suffer from small event scales, exact and near-duplicate messages, lack of location-based filtering for impacted zones, and absent standardized test splits, which prevents researchers from rigorously training and benchmarking modern data-hungry deep learning models for humanitarian disaster management.
domain: Crisis Informatics, Natural Language Processing, Disaster Response and Management, Social Media Text Classification
theoretical_framework: Crisis informatics taxonomy and humanitarian information requirements grounded in the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (UN OCHA) Multi-Cluster/Sector Initial Rapid Assessment (MIRA) framework, situational awareness theory in emergency response, and inter-coder reliability theory (Fleiss' kappa, Krippendorff's alpha, and majority agreement metrics).
methodology: The authors created a standardized data collection, filtering, crowdsourcing, and benchmarking pipeline comprising: (1) streaming keyword and hashtag data collection through the AIDR platform across 19 major disaster events (2016–2019) capturing 24,859,155 raw tweets; (2) a multi-stage filtering pipeline incorporating event date bounding, geographic filtering (prioritizing GPS coordinates, followed by place bounding boxes, and OpenStreetMap/Nominatim user profile geocoding), English language filtering, classifier-based pre-filtering with a Random Forest model (F1 = 76.9%) to prune non-humanitarian messages, minimum token length thresholds (greater than or equal to three words or hashtags), and cosine similarity de-duplication on uni-gram and bi-gram term-frequency vectors (threshold 0.75) reducing the collection to 337,082 candidate tweets; (3) class-balanced random sampling yielding 109,612 tweets for annotation; (4) crowdsourced Amazon Mechanical Turk annotation with 10-tweet qualification tests, embedded gold standard check tweets in 30-tweet HITs (requiring at least 70% accuracy), and a 66% inter-annotator consensus threshold across 11 humanitarian categories yielding 77,196 agreed labeled tweets; and (5) supervised multiclass classification benchmarking across event-level, event-type-level, and all-combined splits (70% train, 10% development, 20% test) comparing classical algorithms (Random Forest and Support Vector Machines with TF-IDF n-gram features) against deep learning architectures (fastText, BERT, DistilBERT, RoBERTa, and XLM-RoBERTa).
datasets: HumAID: 77,196 human-annotated English tweets (76,484 tweets utilized in benchmark classification tasks across 10 humanitarian categories after pruning low-prevalence classes with fewer than 15 samples) covering 19 natural disaster events across four disaster types (earthquakes, wildfires, floods, and hurricanes/cyclones) between 2016 and 2019
AIDR 24.8M Raw Disaster Tweet Stream: 24,859,155 raw tweets collected via Twitter Streaming API across 19 disaster events
Pre-trained fastText Common Crawl Word Embeddings
Pre-trained Transformer Checkpoints: BERT (bert-base-uncased), DistilBERT (distilbert-base-uncased), RoBERTa (roberta-base), and XLM-RoBERTa (xlm-roberta-base)
key_findings: Transformer-based pretrained language models consistently outperform classical machine learning algorithms (Random Forest and Support Vector Machines) and fastText across individual disaster events, disaster event types, and the combined dataset.

Monolingual RoBERTa achieved the highest overall average performance with a weighted F1-score of 0.781, outperforming XLM-RoBERTa (0.777), DistilBERT (0.769), BERT (0.768), fastText (0.712), SVM (0.710), and Random Forest (0.700).

DistilBERT achieved classification performance comparable to BERT (average weighted F1 of 0.769 compared to 0.768) while operating with substantially fewer parameters and lower computational overhead, establishing DistilBERT as an effective architecture for latency-sensitive operational deployment.

Monolingual pretraining in RoBERTa yielded higher performance on English disaster tweets than multilingual pretraining in XLM-RoBERTa, although XLM-RoBERTa demonstrated strong competitive capability across all disaster categories.

Support Vector Machines outperformed Random Forest across almost all event configurations (0.710 versus 0.700 average weighted F1), demonstrating competitive performance relative to fastText (0.712 weighted F1).

The systematic filtering pipeline (date boundaries, geographic resolution, relevance pre-filtering, token length pruning, and cosine similarity de-duplication) successfully eliminated redundant noise and out-of-area chatter from 24.8 million tweets, yielding moderate to substantial inter-annotator agreement (average Fleiss' kappa of 0.55, Krippendorff's alpha of 0.57, and majority agreement of 0.83).
scope_and_delimitations: The corpus is delimited strictly to English-language tweets collected from the Twitter streaming API via the AIDR platform.

The research scope is restricted to 19 sudden-onset natural disaster events occurring between 2016 and 2019 across four disaster categories (earthquakes, wildfires, floods, and hurricanes/cyclones) that directly affected land and caused major damage.

The annotation framework enforces a single-label mutually exclusive classification task per tweet across 11 predefined humanitarian categories, deliberately omitting multi-label assignments to optimize crowdworker annotation budgets.

Benchmark classification experiments excluded low-prevalence classes containing fewer than 15 samples per event, reducing the experimental benchmark pool from 77,196 tweets to 76,484 tweets across 10 evaluable humanitarian categories.

limitations.verbatim_excerpt: We choose to only annotate English tweets due to budget limitations. Therefore, we discard all non-English tweets using the Twitter provided language metadata for a given tweet. It would be interesting to annotate tweets in other languages in future studies. Though multiple labels can be assigned to a tweet, however, we limited it to one category to reduce the annotation efforts.
limitations.summary: The authors acknowledge key constraints in their research design: (1) annotation was limited strictly to English-language tweets due to budgetary restrictions, omitting non-English crisis communications; (2) tweets were assigned a single mutually exclusive category despite microblog messages frequently containing multi-faceted situational information; and (3) low-prevalence classes with fewer than 15 instances were removed from specific event evaluation benchmarks.

generalizability_gap: The dataset and benchmark models focus exclusively on English-language Twitter messages across four types of natural disasters (earthquakes, wildfires, floods, and hurricanes/cyclones). Consequently, the empirical findings and trained models may not generalize to non-English or code-switched crisis messages, human-induced emergencies (such as industrial accidents, acts of terrorism, or armed conflicts), slow-onset crises (such as droughts or famines), or alternative social media and messaging platforms (such as Facebook, Telegram, WhatsApp, or Sina Weibo).
methodological_gap: The study employs a mutually exclusive single-label formulation that cannot capture multi-intent disaster messages containing both urgent supply requests and infrastructural damage reports. In addition, geographic filtering relies on user-provided profile metadata for the 98% of tweets lacking GPS coordinates, which introduces potential location noise and geographical selection bias. Furthermore, the pipeline utilizes an automated Random Forest pre-filter that may discard borderline humanitarian messages prior to human crowdsourcing.
future_work: Annotating disaster tweets in non-English and low-resource languages to broaden linguistic coverage in crisis informatics.
Conducting cross-event and cross-disaster-type transfer learning and domain adaptation experiments using the standardized public benchmark splits.
Developing multimodal classification architectures that jointly analyze disaster tweet text and accompanying crisis imagery.
Extending annotation taxonomies and machine learning architectures to support multi-label crisis classification.
Deploying and evaluating computationally lightweight transformer models, such as DistilBERT, within real-time streaming disaster relief pipelines.
